seo_title: Grandson's Claim in Father's Inherited Property: SC Rules
title: Can a Grandson Claim a Share in Property His Father Inherited? The Supreme Court Says No
meta_description: A November 2026 Supreme Court ruling on Section 8 of the Hindu Succession Act: why a grandson has no birthright in property his father inherited.
intro: A man dies leaving a plot of land, survived by his son and no will. Under the Hindu Succession Act, the son inherits it. Years later, while the son is still alive and has done nothing more than hold onto the property, his own son, the original owner's grandson, files a suit claiming a half share in it, arguing that property coming down from a grandfather is ancestral property in which a grandson acquires a right the moment he is born. On 6 November 2026, the Supreme Court rejected exactly this argument.

The case is J. Rajesh (Minor), through his mother and natural guardian, v. M. Kumaran (since deceased, through legal representatives), reported as 2026 INSC 1208. It turns on Section 8 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, the default rule for what happens to a Hindu male's property when he dies without a will, and it answers a question that comes up often in Indian families: once a father inherits property from his own father under the general law of succession, does the property carry any built-in claim for the father's children, or can the father deal with it as he alone wishes. This guide explains the ruling and what it means as on November 2026.

sections.heading: The Facts the Court Was Dealing With
paragraphs: The dispute traced back to land in Chennai that had belonged to the grandfather. After his death, the land passed to his son under Section 8 of the Hindu Succession Act, since he died intestate. The grandson, a minor represented by his mother, filed a suit through his guardian claiming a half share in the property, framing the claim as one where his father's share was, in his submission, ancestral property in which he had a coparcenary right by birth, entitling him to a share even while his father was still alive and had not transferred or divided the property.

The Madras High Court had ruled against the grandson in a judgment dated 11 August 2010, and the matter reached the Supreme Court as Civil Appeal No. 7020 of 2012, decided more than a decade later by a bench of Justices Augustine George Masih and Sunita Agarwal. The Court dismissed the appeal, upholding the result the High Court had reached: that the grandson's suit, filed while his father was alive, had no basis.

sections.heading: Why Section 8 Settles the Question Against the Grandson
paragraphs: Section 8 is the general rule governing how a Hindu male's property devolves when he dies without a will. The property goes first to his Class I heirs, a list that in this case included his son. The Supreme Court treated Section 8 as a self-contained, complete code for this situation, meaning the property that reaches an heir under Section 8 is that heir's own property, held in his individual right, and not something that automatically becomes joint family or ancestral property in the hands of the next generation merely because it originally came from the grandfather.

The practical consequence is that a son who inherits property under Section 8 is free to deal with it, sell it, mortgage it, gift it, or leave it by will, without needing his own children's consent, and without his children acquiring any right by birth in it while he is alive. The Court held that neither Section 6 of the Hindu Succession Act, which deals with coparcenary property and the rights of daughters in it after the 2005 amendment, nor a Tamil Nadu state amendment the appellant relied on, changed this result on the facts of the case, since both provisions address a different kind of property from what an individual heir takes under Section 8.

sections.heading: How This Differs From True Coparcenary Property
paragraphs: The distinction the ruling turns on is an old one in Hindu law, between property a person inherits from an ancestor in a way that makes it joint family property from the outset, carrying rights for the next generation by birth, and property an individual simply inherits under the statute in their own right. Property passing by survivorship within an undivided Hindu joint family, where it existed before a partition, is treated differently from property that devolves on an individual heir under the testamentary or intestate succession rules the Act itself sets out.

Once Section 8 is the route by which the property reached the son, rather than survivorship within a continuing joint family, the Court's reasoning treats the result as settled: the property is the son's individual property. A grandson cannot get around this by arguing that the land was, in a general sense, inherited from a grandfather and therefore counts as ancestral. The source of the property matters less than the specific legal route by which it passed to the current holder.

sections.heading: What This Means for a Family Still Holding Such Property
paragraphs: For a father who inherited property this way and is now considering a sale, a gift, or a will that leaves it unevenly between his children, this ruling removes one argument his children might otherwise raise against him while he is alive: that they already have a vested share simply by virtue of being born into the family. It does not, on its own, prevent a child from making other claims later, for instance after the father's own death, when the property becomes part of his estate and ordinary succession or will-based rules apply to it in the usual way.

For a grandchild weighing a similar claim, the lesson runs the other way: a suit filed while the parent who holds the property is still alive, and has still not partitioned or transferred it, is likely to fail on exactly this ground, that no right by birth exists in property the parent holds as individual property under Section 8. The timing matters, since the position after the parent's own death, when the property passes again under the Act's rules, is a separate question this ruling does not resolve either way.

sections.heading: A Word on the Broader 2026 Pattern in Succession Cases
paragraphs: This ruling sits alongside a string of 2026 Supreme Court decisions narrowing arguments that try to stretch inherited property into automatically shared family wealth across generations. The idea running through these cases is that the Act's specific devolution rules, rather than a general cultural sense of property staying within the family, decide who owns what and when the next generation's rights, if any, actually arise. A family relying on informal assumptions about ancestral property, rather than checking which provision of the Act actually governed how a given property passed down, is the one most likely to be surprised by how a court eventually resolves the question.

The confusion is understandable, because the word ancestral gets used loosely in everyday conversation to mean anything that has been in the family for more than one generation, while the courts use it in a far narrower technical sense tied to how the property actually devolved. A family that wants certainty should work out, for each significant asset, the exact route by which the current holder came to own it: did it pass by survivorship in an undivided joint family that has never been partitioned, or did it reach the current holder as an individual heir under the statute's own rules. The two routes look similar from the outside but carry very different consequences for the next generation.

sections.heading: Practical Lessons for Wills and Family Settlements
paragraphs: A person who inherited property under Section 8 and wants to avoid a dispute of exactly this kind after their own death should say so plainly in a will or a family settlement deed, recording how the property was acquired and that it is held as individual, self-acquired property rather than joint family property, rather than leaving the next generation to reconstruct the history from old revenue or registration records years later. A family settlement that divides such property unevenly between children, or leaves one child out altogether, is on firmer ground once the deed itself records that the property was the deceased's individual property and not ancestral property in which the children already held a birth right.

A grandchild who believes they do have a genuine claim, for instance because the property in question actually did pass by survivorship in a joint family that was never partitioned, rather than through an individual inheritance under Section 8, should gather the documentary history early: old partition deeds, revenue records, and any earlier litigation about the same property, since this ruling shows that a court will look closely at exactly how the property came down before accepting that a birth right exists at all.

faqs.q: If my father inherited land from my grandfather, do I automatically have a share in it?
faqs.a: Not while your father is alive, according to the Supreme Court's ruling in J. Rajesh v. M. Kumaran (2026 INSC 1208). Property your father inherited under Section 8 of the Hindu Succession Act is his individual property, and you acquire no right in it by birth simply because it originally came from your grandfather.

faqs.q: Can my father sell or will away property he inherited from his father without my consent?
faqs.a: Generally yes, because the property is treated as his individual property once it devolves on him under Section 8 of the Hindu Succession Act, and he does not need his children's consent to deal with it while he is alive.

faqs.q: Does this ruling affect my rights after my father dies?
faqs.a: No, the ruling concerns a claim filed while the property-holding parent is still alive. Once your father dies, the property becomes part of his estate, and ordinary succession rules, or his will if he leaves one, determine what you receive, separately from the question this ruling decided.

faqs.q: Is there a difference between ancestral property and property my father inherited under Section 8?
faqs.a: Yes. Property that remains joint family property by survivorship, from before any partition, works differently from property an individual heir takes under the Act's own devolution rules. The Supreme Court treated property reaching a son under Section 8 as his individual property, not automatically joint family property.

faqs.q: Does a Tamil Nadu-specific coparcenary amendment change this result?
faqs.a: Not on the facts of this case. The Supreme Court held that neither the Tamil Nadu amendment the appellant relied on nor Section 6 of the Hindu Succession Act altered the outcome, since both provisions address a different category of property from what the son held under Section 8.
